display_title: Official Review of Paper4193 by Reviewer eaJk

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes Gradient Assisted Learning, a method for decentralized supervised learning without sharing data, models, and objective functions among different organizations. It generalized Assisted Learning to allow private local training model and objective function, and parallel aggregations across multiple organizations. The authors develop GAL algorithm, provides asymptotic convergence analysis, and experimental results that shows the performance of GAL is close to centralized learning results.
content.main_review:
Strength

1) The proposed GAL approach is novel for allowing parallel optimization among assisting organizations, and generalizing loss functions.
2) The authors provides comprehensive experiments, both classification and regression, to show the effectiveness of proposed GAL algorithm v.s. AL and VAFL. 

Weakness

1) The authors advocates GAL over AL on reducing number of communication rounds and parallel optimization, and as a result has low communication and network costs. It would be great if the authors can provide the computational times in the experiment section to quantify the time-saving advantages of GAL decentralized learning.
2) The authors claim that GAL significantly outperforms AL, and I only find one example from the paper which supports that (e.g. MIMIC3). It would be a more convincing statement if the same observation holds for the other two regression datasets (Diabetes/Boston Housing). The same goes for the computational time for GAL v.s. VAFL, as their accuracies on ModelNet40 don't differ much.


Some typos:
1) page 3, last paragraph, E_{N}L_1(y,F_1(x_1)) --> E_{N}L_1(y_1,F_1(x_1))
2) page 4, second paragraph, a continuous - valued vector r_1 = [r_{i,1}]_{i=1}^N \in R^{N \times k}, what is k here? number of classes for a classification task?
3) page 8, caption of figure 4, MIMIC3 (d-e) --> MIMIC3 (d-f)
3) page 8, second last paragraph, 1) GAL requires much less number -->  2) GAL requires much less number
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall I vote for accepting. I like the novelty of the proposed GAL algorithm on parallel optimization across assisting organizations, and generalization of loss function over AL. My major request is more evidence for supporting statements that GAL outperforms AL, and GAL is computationally more efficient than AL and VAFL.

content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

We compare our computation and communication cost with other baseline methods in Table 3 in the revision. 1) Compared with AL under the same communication cost constraint, our method requires 1/M communication rounds. It is due to that AL trains local models one after another in a sequential manner. Specifically, the Alice of AL first trains its local model and broadcasts its residual to the first collaborator. The first collaborator fits the residual and transmits the output back to Alice, who will then broadcast a new residual to the second collaborator, and so on. Therefore, one assistance round of AL requires $M$ communication rounds to traverse $M$ organizations once. However, one assistance round of our method only requires one communication round because we can train every organization and aggregate their outputs in parallel.

Also, our major advantage over VAFL and vertical federated learning works is that we significantly reduce the number of communication rounds. Compared with VAFL and other vertical FL methods, our method requires far fewer communication rounds because we allow more local training by saving intermediate models at each assistance round. In particular, VAFL requires a batch-wise update from the server. The batch size of VAFL is 0.01 of the whole dataset, then 100 training epochs would result in 10000 communication rounds for each organization. The communication cost of VAFL is $O(d\cdot E_m)$ while the communication cost of GAL is $O(K\cdot T)$ where $d,E_m,K,T$ represent the size of feature embeddings, the number of training epochs of organization $m$, the size of target labels, and the number of assistance rounds respectively. display_title: Further clarifications

content.title: Further clarifications
content.comment:
1. We point out that storing multiple local models reduces the communication coordination among organizations and allow organizations to train different local models.

**Reduce communication coordination** During the learning stage, our method significantly outperforms VAFL in terms of the number of communication rounds (from ~10000 to ~10). We believe computation storage is less of a concern for organizational learners who have sufficient computation resources. We focus on reducing the required level of coordination among organizational learners by allowing more local training and less communication. This is also the motivation of AL, and both AL and GAL require to store multiple local models. An example to illustrate the importance of reducing communication coordination can be found in the breakthrough from FedSGD (transmit and aggregate gradient for every data batch) to FedAvg (transmit model parameters trained for multiple epochs). During the prediction stage, we want to recall that we only require each organization to transmit **once**. In particular, during the prediction stage, each organization will forward their data to local models across multiple assistance rounds and transmit the outputs to Alice to produce overarching output. Therefore, our method does not introduce any additional dependence among organizations.

 **Local model architecture** Another advantage of GAL over VAFL is that by storing local models, we allow each organization to choose its own model architecture. This merit inherited from AL allows Alice to train a linear model while others can train decision trees, SVMs, or neural networks considering their own computation and technical resources. On the contrary, VAFL and other vertical FL methods rely on backward propagation from the server and a globally shared parametric model like neural networks, which is quite restrictive.

We do not have access to the source code of VAFL. As VAFL is a federated version of intermediate data fusion, we assume that VAFL performs slightly worse than the 'Interm' case and thus should be comparable with the result of GAL.

2. Our contribution of private loss functions mainly focuses on the overarching loss $L_1$ (of Alice, who is being assisted). We agree that it is better to include results of the alignment of different local loss functions. We present an ablation study of local loss functions ($M=8$) below. Recall in Section 4 (Learning) that we use $l_1$ for regression task and $l_2$ for classification task. In this study, we use different regression functions $l_q(y, \hat{y})=|y-\hat{y}|^q$ where $q\in\{1,1.5,2,4\}$. For ($l_{q_1}, l_{q_2}$), half of organizations including Alice use $l_{q_1}$ while the other half use $l_{q_2}$. The results show that regression and classification tasks can generally work with various types and combinations of local loss functions. Some classification datasets like Blob and QSAR only work well with $q>1$; we believe it is due to that $l_1$ does not give enough penalty for data points classified incorrectly.

display_title: Official Review of Paper4193 by Reviewer bj7h

content.summary_of_the_paper:
Setting: data is partitioned vertically across firms and each firm has a proprietary ML task they aim to solve. 

The authors propose a method how the firms can assist each other in improving their service without sharing their data, models or training objectives.
The procedure generalizes gradient boosting and works as follows: Firm A fits a model using its local data. Then it computes the residual for each sample and shares this with the other firms. These firms fit the residual and share their predictions. Firm A then finds the optional weights to weight these predictions to best fit the residual for its local loss. The weights are stored, the residual is again computed and the procedure is repeated. At test time firm A needs to collect all the predictions of the residual models in order to aggregate them using the stored weights.  
An asymptotic optimality result is provided and empirically the method is compared to several baselines for different models and datasets. The authors conclude that their method offers competing performance to existing methods while requiring less communication.
content.main_review:
**Strength**

-	The paper is easy to follow and the procedure is well explained. 
-	Collective learning without sharing data or models is an important problem.

**Weaknesses**

The term assisted learning is a bit misleading and the procedure has important limitations that make it very unpractical. I would like to be convinced that there are setting where the required level of coordination is feasible.

i) Assistance is not only required during training but also for every inference task. The procedure does not help firm A to train a better predictor, it only learns how to aggregate the residual predictions of other firms. This implies that it heavily relies on the other models being available for any inference task and having access to the respective features of the individual that needs to be predicted. 

ii) You are not only asking additional training from other firms, but you ask them to store all the intermediate models trained to help firm A and these models need to be ready to be queried on demand. These models do not have any other purpose, so this is quite a lot to ask for.

iii) In each round you rely on each firm having access to different features of the same N samples. Furthermore you need to identify the individuals so you can match the different predictions. Could you justify scenarios where this is realistic to assume?

*Some clarifying questions and comments*

1. The role of the loss function for fitting the residual is not discussed much. Since you do not want to reveal the loss function, the residuals could be fit using a different loss function that the target. My intuition is that, in the spirit of boosting, you will be fine as long as the prediction provide some information gain. I would expect that the more the objectives are aligned the fewer boosting rounds you need. 

 - Could you elaborate more on how different these loss functions can be from the target objective and what is beneficial for learning? 
 - In your theoretical analysis what is the role of the assumption that L be in the spam of the organization specific function classes?  I would appreciate some intuition.

2. You extend AL to train multiple organizations in parallel. Why do you want this? It seems to me that you need to demand less compute, storage and communication from each firm if you would fit them sequentially, which is what you care about. Or is this intuition not correct? I am not convinced by the claim that GAL is much better than AL.
3. Can you give an example where you do not want to reveal your loss function because of privacy reasons?
4. One of the main motivation for your method is to reduce communication. It would be nice is you could provide more discussion about the communication cost of your method in comparison to the baselines and evaluate or quantify it for the empirical results you provide.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The paper is well written, the description of the method is clear and the idea to parallelize the residual computation in boosting without coordinating on the loss to be used seems novel. However I have a couple of questions and I am concerned that the proposed model of cooperation is highly unpractical so that the advantage of reducing communication costs is not significant enough to justify the required compromises. 

If the authors can convince me otherwise and address my questions I am willing to increase my score.

display_title: Further clarifications Part 1

content.title: Further clarifications Part 1
content.comment:
We thank your time and valuable comments. We address each of your concerns below. Please let us know if anything needs further clarifications. Thank you.

i)-iii)  We address your comment from two points.  
 a) We require each organization to store multiple models because it allows us to significantly reduce the communication rounds during training compared with the vertical FL method, as demonstrated in Table 3. Each model solves a small part of the overarching loss at each communication round, so we can consistently decrease or maintain the training loss from the previous communication round. On the contrary, vertical FL methods like VAFL rely on FedSGD and require batchwise transmission of gradients. Therefore, the training loss of VAFL can oscillate across different communication rounds due to the instability nature of FedSGd.  
b) Following your comment, we have now updated Table 3 with 'Computation Space.' In practice, our approach makes a trade-off between communication complexity and computation space. Both AL and GAL require the same computation space to store local models across $T=10$ assistance rounds. Still, GAL is better than AL in terms of prediction performance, communication rounds, and computation time. Compared with VAFL, our method requires storing $T \times$ local models during the learning stage, but GAL can significantly reduce the communication rounds and communication cost. Finally, we note that our modeling is progressive, meaning that we can always train with more but test with fewer assistance rounds.       

1. We first address your comment on how good the best function in the span performs. Our theory focuses on the convergence analysis that with suitable control of the learning rates, the abstract form of GAL can converge to the best one could obtain within the span. An implication of the result is that GAL can significantly improve upon single-organization learning. In particular, suppose that the first organization ($m=1$) does not collaborate with others. A corollary of our result is the convergence for that particular organization $\lim_{t\rightarrow \infty} L(F_t) = inf_{f \in span(F1)} L(f)$. It can be seen that the GAL will produce a significant gain for this organization as long as the infimum of $L_1$ over  $span(F1,\ldots,F_M)$ is larger than that over $span(F1)$, which is likely to occur since $span(F1)$ is within $span(F1,\ldots,F_M)$ and $F_i$ ($i \neq 1$) is operated on different data modalities (with rich side information).  
On the other hand, we could make an additional assumption that the best function (in the sense of minimizing $L_1$) that operates on the centralized data in hindsight falls into the $span(F1,\ldots,F_M)$. Under such an assumption, $L_1$ not only performs "good"` but also performs "the best". Nevertheless, we note that this assumption is somewhat strong. If the assumption does not hold, the best we could do is to find $f$ that attains the limit within the span, due to the limitation that organizations cannot share data and our proposed mechanism of collaboration among organizations.  
We then address your comment on the role of $\ell_m$. It does not appear in our theoretical analysis, because we developed the convergence analysis by considering an abstract form of the GAL training procedure, as described in Algorithm 2 on page 18. Therefore, the $\ell_m$ is absorbed in the abstract form of Equation (4), where we assume that the functional gradient descent can be solved at a population level. In practical implementations, we use $\ell_m$ only as machinery to approximate the pseudo-residual at each round.

content.title: Further clarifications Part 2
content.comment:
2. Following your comment, we have updated table 3 for a better explanation. We clarify that the result of 'Benchmark' for MIMIC3 and 'MVCNN' for ModelNet40 are obtained from the papers using centralized training ($M=1$). We use different $M$ for VAFL because we do not have access to their source code, and what we can do is to refer to the results reported in the original paper where they use $M=4$ for the ModelNet40 dataset. We choose the same number of training epochs because we want a fair comparison among different methods in terms of computation time, computation space, communication rounds, and communication cost. As illustrated from the learning curves in the figures, most of our results converge within $~3$ assistance rounds even though we train for $10$ assistance rounds.  
Please note that we require ``much less`` communication complexity than AL and VAFL. There is no communication cost of 'Benchmark' and 'MVCNN' because they are centralized baselines. As mentioned in i)-iii), our approach makes a trade-off between communication complexity and computation space. AL and GAL require the same computation space, but GAL outperforms AL in terms of prediction performance, communication rounds, and computation time. AL requires $T \times$ computation space compared with VAFL, but it significantly reduces the communication rounds and communication cost due to that VAFL requires batchwise gradient update. Our prediction results are also progressive, which means that our method can adjust the assistance rounds during the prediction stage to strike a balance between communication and performance.

content.title: conclusion from discussion
content.comment:
I thank the reviews for engaging with my concerns and adding clarifying comments to the manuscript. I will increase the score by one point so that someone else can champion the paper if they want. However I am not happy with the answer to my first point and my initial concerns regarding the practicality of the method mostly remain.

1.	**allowing for private loss functions at each organization**. You claim this as a technical novelty over assisted learning. I think this is an interesting extension but if you claim it as a technical contribution it should be discussed and analyzed more carefully. In your algorithm you allow for objectives that are not aligned but neither your theory nor your experiments are investigating the implications of this. Other reviewers have raised this concern as well and I could not find a satisfactory answer.  It is not clear under what conditions this works and what degree of alignment you need in practice. Without assumptions you cannot guarantee any gain from asking for assistance, you can only guarantee that it is non-negative with a perfect line search procedure. Other agents might mess up your model if they use an inappropriate loss function, but you will just end up assigning a step-size of zero to their update. What regime are you in with a practical setup? How large are the gains if your private objective is complex but others only use a standard square loss? An investigation of how the gain and the alignment of the loss functions correlate, either empirically or analytically would be necessary here.

2.	**Practicality**. I see that the challenge of aligning the data points and relying on availability of other agents for inference is faced by previous works on assisted learning too, so I don’t want to judge practicality solely on this.  But I am still concerned that your method is introducing additional practical challenges - fitting and storing multiple residual models to assist a single organization is a lot of overhead and introduces a very high dependence between agents. A concrete example where all this is feasible would be nice to add.

display_title: About Practicality

content.title: About Practicality
content.comment:
1) Aligning the data points and relying on availability of other agents is also faced by vertical federated learning methods and data fusion methods in general. 
2) We do not introduce more dependence between agents compared with AL and VAFL. First, based on our results, we think it is fair to say that our method dominantly outperforms AL in all aspects including prediction, communication and computation. Second, VAFL also assists a single organization and the only overhead of our method compared with VAFL is computation storage but not dependence among organizations. We point out that storing multiple local models reduces the communication coordination among organizations and allow organizations to train different local models.

a) **Reduce communication coordination** During learning stage, our method significantly outperforms VAFL in terms of the number of communication rounds (from ~10000 to ~10). We believe computation storage is less of concern for organizational learners who have sufficient computation resources. We focus on reducing the required level of coordination among organizational learners by allowing more local training and less communication. This is also the motivation of AL and both AL and GAL require to store multiple local models. An example to illustrate the importance of reducing communication coordination can be found in the breakthrough from FedSGD (transmit and aggregate gradient for every data batch) to FedAvg (transmit model parameters trained for multiple epochs). During prediction stage, we want to recall that we only require each organization to transmit **once**. In particular, during prediction stage, each organization will forward their data to local models across multiple assistance rounds and transmit the outputs to Alice to produce overarching output. Therefore, we disagree that our method introduce any additional dependence among organizations.

b) **Local model architecture** Another advantage of GAL over VAFL is that by storing local models, we allow each organization to choose its own model architecture. This merit inherited from AL allows Alice to train a linear model while others can train decision trees, SVMs, or neural networks considering their own computation and technical resources. On the contrary, VAFL and other vertical FL methods rely on backward propagation from the server and a globally shared parametric model like neural networks, which is quite restrictive.

Our method is possibly the most practical method focusing on vertically distributed data. We do not claim that our work resolves the problem of vertically distributed data once and for all. However, we believe it is not reasonable to reject us only because of the practical concern of storing local models. First, storing local models is inherited from previous published works, Gradient Boosting and Assisted Learning. It takes years for Gradient Boosting to develop from a methodology paper to a mature and popular tool like XGBoost. A future application is to build a software package to wrap up local models so that the users can regard them as a single model in the hindsight. Second, storing local models actually reduces communication coordination and allows flexible local model architecture as mentioned above in (a) and (b). We hope the reviewer can revise the score based on our response and revision as appropriate.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper considers the distributed learning scenario where the underlying entities may have little interest in sharing their data, proprietary models and objective functions. The authors propose a new method, Gradient Assisted Learning (GAL) , as a strategy for other entities to assist each other without sharing data, models, and objective functions.
content.main_review:
This paper studies an interesting distributed setting where entities could help each other. This paper is well written and easy to follow. Experiments are extensive. I also have the following concerns.  

1. The distributed setting considered in this paper is novel but may have some practical shortcomings. For example, for other entities, we need them to fit the “residuals”, which essentially requires regression objective functions. Does it mean that only entities with regression objective functions can assist the target entity? Furthermore, if most entities use classification objective functions, which is possible because of the variety of classification tasks, the benefits of the proposed method might be limited. I am quite worried that the proprietary loss functions at other entities may not be compatible with the residual fitting loss. 

2. The residual that needs to be approximated from Equation 2 is defined over distribution over all features p_{x,y}. Since Alice does not have access to all features, it’s not clear how the residual is computed.  

3. Two sub-optimization problems need to be solved at each round in order to get weights $\hat{w}_t$ and learning rate $\hat{\eta}^t$.  
More discussion on how costly it is to solve them could be very helpful. 

4. In the second paragraph of Section 3.2, what is y in the formula for $F_{Alone}$ and $F_{Joint}$? Is it a typo for $y_1$?

content.title: Thank you for the time and comments. We address each comment below.
content.comment:
1. We want to first clarify that any learner can play two roles, to be assisted or to assist others. In our paper, without loss of generality, we supposed that learner 1 (Alice) is the one to be assisted, whose loss ($L_1$) is named the overarching objective function. Our framework does not restrict the choice of overarching objective functions as long as it is differentiable. Other learners provide assistance with local (regression) loss functions $\ell_m$ for fitting the residuals, but not for the overarching objective functions. The choice of $L_1$ does not depend on $\ell_m$, and vice versa. If another organization $i$ wants to be assisted, it can define its own overarching objective function $L_i$ while other collaborators can assist organization $i$ with local regression objective functions $\ell_m$.

2. We do not need the complete data to compute the residuals. Initially, we first compute the initial state as the unbiased estimate of target labels, namely $F^0(x) = \mathbb{E}_N(y_1)$. We compute the residuals as $r_1^1= - \left[\frac{\partial L_1\left(y_1, F^{0}(x)\right)}{\partial F^{0}(x)}\right]$. Then, we train local models to fit the residual. Next, we combine the initial state and the outputs of local models to obtain $F^1(x)$ at assistance round $1$. After that, we can compute the residual for the second assistance round as $r_1^2= - \left[\frac{\partial L_1\left(y_1, F^{1}(x)\right)}{\partial F^{1}(x)}\right]$. Note that we only need the predicted outputs and target labels to compute the residual.

3. The cost to solve for the optimal gradient assistance weights $w$ and gradient assisted learning rate $\eta$ is negligible compared with the cost to solve for the pseudo residuals because the number of parameters to optimize is very small, namely $w \in \mathbb{R}^{M}$ and $\eta \in \mathbb{R}^{1}$. Following your comment, we have added related discussions in the revision.

4. It should be $y_1$. We have fixed the typo in the revision.

content.comment:
Thanks the authors for further clarification. I am sorry that I am still concerned with the first point. 

To further clarify, when learner 1 requests for assistance, is it true that learner 1 (Alice) can only get assistance from other learners that have the regression objective among their proprietary loss functions? In other words, if another learner does not have regression objective among its proprietary loss functions, this learner cannot assist learner 1 (Alice) ?

display_title: Further clarification

content.title: Further clarification
content.comment:
Dear Reviewer 2f2X, thank you for the excellent question. The short answer is that learner 1 (Alice) can get assistance from any other learners. We elaborate on the subtleties below. 

1. The term "proprietary loss function" can be interpreted in two ways. First, any learner who seeks assistance (e.g., Alice) has an overarching loss that is proprietary, denoted by $L$ in our paper. This proprietary loss is of primary interest since it is directly related to the ultimate task to assist. Alice only locally holds it. Second, any learner who participates in the assistance to Alice will need a loss to approximate the direction of the (functional) gradient, denoted by $\ell$. This loss can be any commonly used regression loss such as the quadratic loss or L1 loss or any sophisticated loss locally developed by that learner. We can also treat the regression loss as "proprietary" because it does not need to be shared with other learners.
2. Overall, the term "proprietary" is mainly for the overarching loss $L$ (of Alice, who is being assisted). For each assisting learner such as Bob, he could always use off-the-shelf regression objectives such as quadratic loss during assisted training. Meanwhile, if he decides to use a local regression objective deemed proprietary, he does not need to share that anyway. 

Please feel free to let us know if the above has addressed your concern. We hope you will view the quality of our paper and revisions favorably. Your support will be much appreciated.

display_title: Official Review of Paper4193 by Reviewer LJjS

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper studies the problem of Assisted Learning (AL) where organizations assist each other to learn supervised tasks without sharing data, model and loss functions. The authors propose a new method Gradient Assisted Learning (GAL) inspired by Gradient Boosting for the vertically distributed federated learning setup. Key contributions include - extending loss functions to more general ones, private loss functions at each organization level and parallel aggregation of outputs from organizations and gradient assistance weights to control learning contribution from each organization. Empirical results show the correctness of the proposed method.
content.main_review:
Overall I like the idea of applying gradient boosted inspired ideas to this problem setup and feel it is novel. It is of practical importance and will be interest to the privacy and federated learning communities. The ideas and technical quality of the paper is good however there is not enough clarity in the background and problem setup (I have outlined some questions I have about my understanding of the setup). I think the authors should give another pass to make these sections clearer. Empirical study is good, but not exhaustive in my opinion and can be made more stronger (more analysis and discussion about why less communication rounds are needed for GAL, discuss the statistical significance of the results). I like the ablation study performed to test the effect of various noise levels and the resulting outcomes from this experiment.

Questions/Comments:
- Problem setup is not fully clear. In section 3.1, it needs to be clearly mentioned what "collaborator" means in this context - does a collaborator have access to part of Alice's data? or labels? or something else too?
- "pseudo-residuals" -> not clear what this means in section 2 and why proposed method needs fewer rounds to converge compared to Federated learning setting. Later on in section 3.3, it is mentioned that Alice broadcasts psuedo residuals to other organizations, but not clear how these are computed (this becomes clear when you look at the algorithm later, but the earlier statement in section 3.3 should also briefly mention it so that the reader is not confused)
- Are each of the organizations going to use the same loss? If yes, what's the need to introduce L_m? If not (which seems to be the case), I do not understand how we measure convergence and residuals when each organization is optimizing a different loss function?
- How much is the cost for each organization to solve the local problem to find the optimal f_m^{t}?
- How much is the cost to solve for the optimal gradient assistance weights w?
- How much is the cost for the line search?
- In the algorithm, I do not understand how the gradient assistance weights are maintained back on the probability simplex? Is there a
projection operation after optimizing these weights that maps them to lie on the simplex?
- In the prediction stage, why is learning rate used while gathering the predictions from multiple organizations?
- What is the intuition behind requiring less assistance rounds?
content.summary_of_the_review: There is some novelty in the proposed GAL algorithm and its inspired roots from Gradient Boosting. It is of practical value to privacy, federated learning and distributed optimization community - thus has a good impact factor. Technical content is good. Presentation and Empirical Study/Discussion are the weaker parts of the paper in my opinion at this point. I feel the authors can make this work stronger after these are addressed.

display_title: Thank you for the time and comments. We address each comment below.

content.title: Thank you for the time and comments. We address each comment below.
content.comment:
1. In the revision, we rephrased the related part of Section 3.1 as "Without loss of generality, we suppose that Alice, the organization to be assisted, has local data $x_1$ and task label $y_1$, while other $M-1$ organizations are collaborators which assist Alice and have local data $x_2 \ldots x_M$." The collaborators do no have access to Alice's data, labels and models. The only things transmitted are Alice's pseudo-residuals and the outputs of the collaborators' local models.

2. Following your comment, we have rewritten the related part in Section 2 and provided an intuitive explanation of "pseudo-residuals" in Subsection 3.2 before it is formally introduced in Subsection 3.3. We also added intuitive explanations as to why the proposed method is expected to have much fewer rounds than FL. Briefly speaking, the FL model training relies on frequent synchronizations of participating clients as each of them contributes to part of the globally shared model. Any local update from a client often does not guarantee a decrease of the global loss. But in our proposed method, each participating organization contributes to a portion of the overarching loss. Thus, each update can reliably decrease the global loss, and it does not need frequent synchronizations. These are intuitions why our method can achieve desirable performance with significantly fewer communication rounds.

3. In the revision, we now emphasize in Algorithm 1 that $\ell_m$ is a local regression loss function for each organization to fit "pseudo-residuals." Each organization can choose its own regression loss functions $\ell_m$. In the experiments, we just let it be the usual squared loss. Meanwhile, we measure the convergence of GAL by monitoring the overarching loss $L_1$ instead of $\ell_m$. When $L_1$ or the gradient assisted learning rate is low, we can stop the training.

4. In our experiments, the number of local training epochs at each communication round is $10$. We find that fewer local training epochs will require more communication rounds to converge. We believe it is a trade-off between the amount of local training and communication. We compare our computation cost with other baseline methods in Table 3 in the revision.

5. The cost to solve for the optimal gradient assistance weights $w$ is negligible compared with the cost to solve for the pseudo residuals, because the number of parameters to optimize is small (since $w \in \mathbb{R}^{M}$). We added the related discussion in the revision.

6. The cost for the line search is negligible compared with the cost to regress the pseudo residuals because the number of parameters to optimize is small (in fact, $\eta \in \mathbb{R}^{1}$). We also mention it in the revision.

7. Yes. We transform the free parameters with a softmax function to maintain them on the probability simplex.

8. The gradient assisted learning rate is a parameter used to combine models from different assistance rounds. In the training stage, they are learned in such way that the aggregated model ensemble performs favorably on the training data. Thus, in the prediction stage, we still use the same aggregation for future data. Also, with a suitable control of the learning rate (as suggested in our theoretical analysis), the aggregated model can be regarded as a good approximation of the oracle model in the span of organizations' local models (in hindsight).

replying_to: Replying to Thank you for the time and comments. We address each comment below.
display_title: Further response

content.title: Further response
content.comment: 9. We have provided some intuitions in our response to your point (b) above (also included in the revision). Moreover, we compare our computation and communication cost with other baseline methods in Table 3 in the revision. Some points are elaborated below. 1) Compared with AL under the same communication cost constraint, our method requires 1/M communication rounds. It is because AL trains local models one after another in a sequential manner. Specifically, in AL, Alice first trains the local model and broadcasts the residual to the first collaborator, then the first collaborator fits the residual and transmits the output back to Alice, who will then broadcast a new residual to the second collaborator, and so on. Therefore, one assistance round of AL requires $M$ communication rounds to traverse $M$ organizations once. However, one assistance round of our method only requires one communication round because we can train every organization and aggregate their outputs in parallel. 2) Compared with VAFL and other vertical FL methods, our method requires far fewer communication rounds because we allow more local training by saving intermediate models at each assistance round. In particular, VAFL requires batch-wise update from the server. The batch size of VAFL is 0.01 of the whole dataset, and 100 training epochs would result in 10000 communication rounds for each organization. In general, the communication cost of VAFL is $O(d\cdot E_m)$ while the communication cost of GAL is $O(K\cdot T)$, where $d,E_m,K,T$ represents the size of feature embeddings, the number of training epochs of organization $m$, the size of target labels, and the number of assistance rounds, respectively. Here, $d$ is typically greater than $K$, and $E_m$ is greater than $T$ because GAL allows more local training. We elaborate on the calculation of those costs in Table 3 of the revision.

content.title: To all reviewers
content.comment:
Thank you for your time and constructive comments. We have addressed all the comments below. The main concern raised in the review comments is that we lack demonstrations of the advantages of GAL over AL and VAFL. The following major changes have been included in the revision. Please let us know if the responses and revisions (colored in blue in the revision) have not addressed any of your concerns.

1. We conduct comprehensive experiments with the baseline method AL for all the 11 datasets. We also show the learning curves of AL in all of our figures. The results indicate that GAL significantly outperforms AL in terms of prediction. We also note that the original AL paper only works for regression tasks with $\eta=1$. We extend it to tackle classification tasks for comparison.

2. We summarize and compare computation and communication cost between GAL and the state-of-the-art methods AL and VAFL in Table 3. We elaborate on the cause of our advantages in Section 4.2. In particular, under the constraint of the same communication cost, GAL outperforms AL in terms of the computation time and the number of communication rounds. Compared with VAFL, GAL significantly reduces the number of communication rounds under the constraint of the same number of local training epochs.
